hook_text: After 1000 coin tosses there were MORE extra heads than after 10. So why do we say luck evens out?
clip_script: Toss a fair coin. After 10 tosses, 7 heads: 2 more than expected, and a fraction of 0.7. Keep going. After 1000 tosses, 512 heads: now 12 more than expected. The extra heads grew. So did luck fail to even out? Look at the fraction instead. 512 out of 1000 is 0.512, almost exactly one half. The fraction settled even though the extra heads did not disappear. The coin never paid back its early heads with bonus tails. Those 12 extra heads just got drowned in a thousand tosses. That is the real law of large numbers: the fraction creeps towards the probability, the count does not have to balance. So the next time someone says tails is due, tell them the coin has no memory and no debts. More tries, closer fraction. Never a payback.
visual_style: A running tally board with columns for tosses, heads and fraction; a broken-line graph zigzags then hugs a glowing one-half line; a counter of extra heads keeps climbing in red beside it; a speech bubble saying tails is due gets crossed out.
pacing: Quick numbers, a pause on the surprising 12, a slow reveal of 0.512, a confident close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to compare relative frequency with probability and tell chance from bias.
